title: The Gurmukh's learning
hook: true learning is reflection on the Name

segments.voice: Yesterday, the river bank: a tree that can fall at any time, so what matters can't wait. Your line was the bank gives way. Did you take the first step? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

A cow lies in the shade, long after she's finished eating, still chewing. Slowly. Thoroughly. Bringing it back up and going over it again until it actually feeds her. Two days ago the Oankar asked the pandit whether he'd understood what he read. Today it answers its own question. If reading and arguing isn't the real thing, what is? The poem's answer has a name, and a person attached to it. Today: the Gurmukh's learning.
screen: `A COW, STILL CHEWING.` → `IF READING ISN'T IT,` → `WHAT IS REAL LEARNING?`

segments.voice: First, the person. The Gurmukh, as we've met all through these weeks, is the one whose face is turned toward the Guru. The opposite, in Gurbani, is the manmukh, the one turned toward their own mind. Both might own the same books. What differs is the direction. Now, the learning. In the Oankar, the Gurmukh's learning is vichar: reflection on the Name. Vichar isn't skimming, and it isn't debating. It's going over a thing again and again, like the cow in the shade, until it feeds you. A pandit's learning, as the poem pictures it, ends in an argument won. A Gurmukh's learning ends somewhere else. Guru Nanak says where in another hymn, in Raga Asa. In paraphrase: when learning is reflected on, a person becomes a benefactor of others. That's a remarkable test for an education. Not how much you know. Not how well you can defend it. Whether it has made you good for the people around you. Reflection, in this teaching, doesn't keep you in your head. It sends you out. Learning that has been chewed long enough turns into kindness, patience, a hand offered. Some Sikhs practice this in an ordinary way: a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, read in the morning, carried and thought over through the day, and talked about with others. The goal isn't to collect lines. It's to let one line work on you until it shows up in what you do. That's the Gurmukh's learning: slow, repeated, and pointed outward.
screen: `GURMUKH: FACE TURNED TO THE GURU.` · `VICHAR: REFLECTION ON THE NAME.` · `LEARNING MAKES YOU GOOD FOR OTHERS.` · `ONE LINE, CHEWED SLOWLY.` · then, large: `REFLECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one line. Take a line from these past days. From the one. Read and understand. The side that bows is the heavier. Or any line from a scripture that matters to you. Say it once, slowly. Then sit with it the way the cow sits with her meal: bring it back, go over it again. On one pass, just hear the words. On the next, let a single word stand out. On the last, let a face come to mind, someone this line could be good for. If your mind wanders, return to the line without fuss. If you pray, you can hold the line as a prayer. If you don't, let it simply be chewed. The bell holds the time.
The Gurmukh's learning. In the Oankar, real learning is vichar, reflection on the Name, and in Guru Nanak's Asa hymn, learning reflected on makes a person good for others. Today's word.
Your line: reflect. Today, carry the line you chose. Bring it back three times, morning, noon and evening, and let it do one good turn for someone. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs reflect on Gurbani through vichar: reading a hymn, hearing it explained in katha at the gurdwara, and thinking it over and discussing it with others.
